Testing for normality? Don't bother

Amy D Willis

Last updated October 20 2026

assumptions.Rmd

A better title: Robust testing and standard errors as an alternative to making false assumptions

In teaching at EBAME this year, I talked about how I strongly prefer “parametric tests” (like t-tests, ANOVA, linear regression, etc) to “non-parametric tests” (like Mann-Whitney, (insert: anova alt), (insert: rank correlation test name)). Participants naturally asked for more resources and justification for this (surprisingly controversial!) viewpoint, inspiring this post.

The smear campaign against “parametric tests”

Fact: t-tests, linear regression, and Poisson regression can be used even if your data are not normally distributed or Poisson distributed.

So,

  • You do not need normally distributed data to perform a t-test
  • You do not need normally distributed, homoskedastic errors to fit, interpret and test hypotheses about linear regression (or ANOVA)
  • You do not need Poisson distributed data to fit Poisson regression

and

  • You do not need check (or formally test) that your data is normally distributed or homoskedastic before performing a t-test
    • (I recommend not assuming equality of variance in your t-test)
  • You do not need check (or formally test) that your residuals are normally distributed or homoskedastic after fitting a linear regression or running an ANOVA
  • You do not need check (or formally test) that your data is Poisson distributed or homoskedastic errors before fitting a Poisson regression

However, you should use “robust standard errors” and “robust hypothesis testing” instead of “model-based standard errors” and “robust hypothesis testing.” These are not returned by default in most statistical software, but are implemented in a number of R packages. I’ll explain them and show you my favourite software below.

Plotting your data is always useful – for quality control, but also because being familiar with your data inspires rigorous science, innovation, and critical thinking! – but a lot of the dogma of “checking assumptions” is 40 years out of date.

Where did the misinformation about come from? Linear and Poisson regression were first developed/invented/derived under distributional assumptions in the early 20th century by the founders of modern statistics. It wasn’t until the 1980’s that mathematical statisticians showed that these assumptions weren’t needed. Some of the key papers were

  • Robust standard errors:
    • White 1980…
  • Consistency of M-estimation
    • …

Somehow, the implications of this work didn’t get distributed far beyond PhDs in statistics, and many people who teach statistics continue to perpetuate the idea that “t-tests and linear regression require unreasonable assumptions.” It’s not true!!

Fact: If your data does follow the distributional assumptions, you can apply the methods, of course! But I’ve never, ever analyzed data that is normally or Poisson distributed, so this is a useless fact in practice, in my view. See below for some comments on efficiency.

Robust errors and tests

While parameter estimates obtained from linear and Poisson regression are just fine, the default standard errors returned by statistical software are not valid if the distributional assumptions don’t apply. That is, usually,

  • model-based standard errors underestimate the true variance in the estimate
  • default p-values have inflated Type 1 error rates

Robust standard errors and robust testing provide a solution to both of these problems. They are called “robust” because they are robust to the distributional assumptions that are assumed by the default (model-based) errors. Essentially, the curvature of the likelihood (which is what determines the variance of an estimator) is estimated from the data rather than imposed by a distributional model.

Here’s one way you can get robust standard errors and robust score tests. For linear regression:

# remotes::install_github("statdivlab/raoBust")
library(tidyverse)
library(raoBust)
data("ddPCR")
ddPCR %>% 
  filter(SpecimenType == "Sputum") %>% 
  glm_test(formula = Value ~ Treatment, 
         data = ., family = gaussian(link = "identity"))
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = Value ~ Treatment, data = ., family = gaussian(link = "identity"))
## 
## 
## Coefficient estimates:
##              Estimate Non-robust Std Error Robust Std Error Lower 95% CI
## (Intercept) 2031812.5             375828.2         400416.7      1247010
## Treatment   -583925.3             933285.6         616926.8     -1793079
##             Upper 95% CI Non-robust Wald p Robust Wald p Robust Score p
## (Intercept)    2816614.8      4.685446e-06  3.890383e-07   0.0001136016
## Treatment       625228.9      5.355927e-01  3.438902e-01   0.3493965173

Results interpretation: We estimate that the average bacterial concentration in Sputum samples is 5.8×1055.8 \times 10^{5} DNA copies/uL lower in participants who received treatment compared to those who did not receive treatment (95% CI: -1.8^{6} to 6.3^{5}, p=0.35).

For logistic regression:

glm_test(formula = presence ~ light, data = light_presence, family = binomial(link = "logit"))
##

## lightLL     -20.74839             3964.631     6.260623e-01    -21.97545

## (Intercept)     20.56607         0.9958611             0   5.465931e-06
## lightLL        -19.52133         0.9958244             0   3.327047e-03

Results interpretation: We estimate that the odds of detecting COG 4251 is e−20.74839≈10−9e^{-20.74839} \approx 10^{-9} times lower in genomes recovered from low light environments compared to genomes recovered from high light environments (95% CI for odds ratio: 2.9^{-10} to 3.3^{-9}, p=p= 0.0033)

My amazing team built raoBust because we kept seeing that robust score tests had better error rates than robust Wald tests, and (shockingly!!) we couldn’t find any software implementing robust score tests – even for simple cases! So, we built one! (Let us know if you have questions or requests for raoBust.)

Other packages R that provide robust standard errors include: sandwich, rigr, others TODO… These give robust Wald tests – far better than model-based testing, but not as good as robust score testing, in my experience.

Why don’t I like non-parametric tests

I like people who perform non-parametric tests (or, most of them!)… but I generally discourage the use of non-parametric tests for the following reasons

  • There is no interpretable parameter
  • They generally test hypotheses that are uninterpretable, and that I don’t care about.

Some theory supporting these claims

I don’t know of a good textbook or paper that makes this point clearly and well – especially in a way useful for microbial ecologists (my target audience). (Maybe I’ll try to get this note published somewhere?)

But the math is straightforward and uses common tools in mathematical statistics… In fact, I can prove them for you quickly here. I do this to write down

The validity of t-tests when the data are not normally distributed

Formal claim: If X1a,X2a,…,XnaaX_1^a, X_2^a, \ldots, X_{n_a}^a are drawn independently from some distribution with mean μa\mu_a and X1b,X2b,…,XnbbX_1^b, X_2^b, \ldots, X_{n_b}^b are drawn independently from some distribution with mean μb\mu_b. Let X‾a=1na∑i=1naXi\bar{X}^a = \frac{1}{n_a} \sum_{i=1}^{n_a} X_i and X‾b=1nb∑i=1nbXi\bar{X}^b = \frac{1}{n_b} \sum_{i=1}^{n_b} X_i . Then

  • X‾b−X‾a\bar{X}^b - \bar{X}^a is an unbiased estimate of μb−μa\mu_b - \mu_a
  • If μa=μb\mu_a = \mu_b , then Pr⁡(|X‾b−X‾a|/sa2/na+sb2/nb>1.96)≈0.05\Pr\left(|\bar{X}_b-\bar{X}_a|/\sqrt{s_a^2/n_a+s_b^2/n_b}>1.96\right)\approx 0.05, and this approximation becomes better and better as nan_a and nbn_b get larger and larger. That is, a t-test with unequal variances controls Type 1 error rates.

The first claim follows from the definition of bias and linearity of expectations. The second follows from the central limit theorem: Xa‾\bar{X^a} is approximately normally distributed, and σâna\frac{\hat{\sigma^a}}{n_a} is a consistent estimate of its variance. Slutsky’s theorem + pivoting gives the result.

Point of emphasis – I did not assume that the XX’s were normally distributed!!

The validity of linear regression when data are not normally distributed

Formal claim: Suppose we observe independent pairs (Xi,Yi)(X_i, Y_i) and mean Yi=β0+β1Xi1+…,βpXip.\text{mean }Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_{i1} + \ldots, \beta_p X_{ip}. Then

  • β̂k\hat{\beta}_k is an unbiased estimate of βk\beta_k
  • If βk=0\beta_k = 0 then Pr(|β̂k|robust std error in β̂k>1.96)=0.05Pr(\frac{|\hat{\beta}_k|}{\text{robust std error in } \hat{\beta}_k} > 1.96) = 0.05

Responding to reviewers who insist on non-parametric tests

I’d probably respond with something like this:

“Please note that (1) the estimates we provided are consistent (asymptotically unbiased) for their target parameters, (2) we reported robust estimates of the standard deviation in the estimates, which do not require parametric assumptions to be valid, and (3) we used robust hypothesis tests to test our hypotheses, which also do not require parametric assumptions to be valid. As a result, our estimates and tests are valid even if our data does not follow a normal distribution (see, e.g., Wakefield (year) Chapter TODO). Briefly, this is because the central limit theorem gives us that means and M-estimators are normally distributed, even if the data is not.”

I’ve found that people tend to back off when they realize they’re talking with someone who knows their shit. Good luck – and feel free to reach out to me by email if took this approach and you’d like me to look over your reviewer response for correctness.
